title: Westbrook Planning Board — Planning Board Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Summarization necessarily condenses and selects; for complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: Chair Larry McWilliams, Vice Chair John Turcotte, Karen Axelson, Nancy Litrocapes, Kevin Price, Robin Tannenbaum, Oriana Farnham (alternate; left at 2:24:07), Lucas Schrage (alternate). Absent: Jason Frazier.

blocks.x: Chair Larry McWilliams called the meeting to order. He reviewed a public-comment policy change discussed at the Sept. 14, 2026 City Council meeting and recommended for the Planning Board as well. Commenters are asked, not required, to state only their name and Westbrook residency rather than a home address. Roll call: six of seven regular members — McWilliams, Vice Chair John Turcotte, Karen Axelson, Nancy Litrocapes, Kevin Price, and Robin Tannenbaum — answered present; Jason Frazier was absent. Both alternates, Oriana Farnham and Lucas Schrage, were seated to fill the vacancy. They alternated votes by agenda item after the minutes, as the chair set out at the start of the meeting.
Quorum (the minimum number of members needed to vote) established.
Approved unanimously by roll call; all eight present, including both alternates, voted yes. Moved by John Turcotte, seconded by Kevin Price.
Administrative Item (not on the printed agenda)
26-000404 — Rock Row South Campus Subdivision Amendment — Extension Request
Not listed on the printed agenda packet — included here because it is part of this meeting's actual record.

Wayne Morrill (Jones & Beach Engineers, for Dirigo Center Developers, LLC) requested a 90-day extension to record a subdivision amendment the board approved June 2, 2026. The applicant is still getting sign-off from the City of Portland, because the parcel crosses the city line. Staff confirmed it only needs to come back to the board for signature, not a new review.

Approved unanimously by roll call, 7–0 — extends the recording deadline to January 28, 2027. All findings/conditions of the June 2, 2026 approval remain valid. Mover not stated on the recording; seconded by Robin Tannenbaum. Oriana Farnham (alternate) did not vote; the alternates took turns by item.

Matthew Peltier (Terradyn Consultants, for Wormell Farms, LLC) requested transferring ~10.02 acres between two commonly-owned lots (Lot 2 and Lot 3 of the former Wormell Farm). The transfer lets Lot 3 meet net-residential-area requirements for a planned ~108-unit apartment project (now called Minnowbrook Apartments). Lot 2's condominium project (59 duplex buildings, under construction) still meets its net-residential requirement after the transfer. Robin Tannenbaum asked for clearer, more legible exhibits on future submittals, and the applicant agreed.
Approved unanimously by roll call, 7–0. Mover not stated on the recording; seconded by Oriana Farnham. Lucas Schrage (alternate) did not vote; the alternates took turns by item.
26-000274 — Site Plan, Subdivision — Rock Row South Campus, Building SG & SR

Dirigo Center Developers, LLC / Waterstone Properties Group presented a 6-story, 277-unit residential building (SR) and a 7-story, 700-space parking garage with ground-level retail (SG). The applicant confirmed the garage is intended to remain free for Rock Row retail customers (subject to change). The applicant also confirmed the team is coordinating with Portland Trails on an underpass/bike-trail connection near the quarry. Building height is capped at 12 stories/150 feet under the zone. City Planner Rebecca Spitella noted the applicant isn't seeking approval tonight, only feedback, pending state permits.

Board voted unanimously, 7–0 by roll call, to continue the application so the applicant can finalize design and incorporate state-permit feedback. Moved by John Turcotte, seconded by Kevin Price. Oriana Farnham (alternate) did not vote; the alternates took turns by item.
26-000777 — Land Use Ordinance Amendment — Data Centers

Staff reviewed the item's history. The City Council enacted a 180-day moratorium, effective June 1, 2026, and expiring late November. It referred the question (sent it for study) to the Planning Board, which held its own workshop last month. The proposed ordinance (a city law) defines and prohibits data centers as a principal use (the main use of a property) citywide. It also removes them from the Rock Row Contract Zone (a special zoning deal for one property), currently the only zone that allows them. It still permits small, on-site "accessory use" server rooms. Member Robin Tannenbaum confirmed with staff that the Rock Row property owner has been informed this isn't necessarily a permanent ban. The land use ordinance can be revisited if a specific future proposal arises.

Board voted unanimously, 7–0 by roll call, to recommend the ordinance amendment to City Council — expected first reading (the first of two required votes) Oct. 19, second reading (the final, binding vote) early November. Moved by Kevin Price, seconded by Oriana Farnham. Lucas Schrage (alternate) did not vote; the alternates took turns by item.

JB Brown & Sons and Westbrook Development Corporation returned with a revised rental project. It has ~306 units, a mix of market-rate and affordable. That is down from an original concept of 800+ units, and from 322 at the last workshop. It sits on ~68 acres between Stroudwater Street and the arterial, near Westbrook Middle School. A workshop item — no approval was requested or voted on tonight.
Why it's this meeting's one real controversy

Nine members of the public spoke. Most objected to routing cars onto two-lane Stroudwater Street (which becomes Westbrook Street in Portland) instead of the limited-access arterial bordering the back of the site. One commenter put the number of additional cars at 500 or more.

“This road can be altered. The idea that it can't be altered is untenable… I'm asking the planning board to give deference to those who have already committed to living in this area… over the convenience of the cost of a developer who probably [isn't] going to live here or live with the consequences.”
blocks.cite: Fred Fowler, Portland resident on Westbrook St. (public comment)

blocks.x: “We're talking about Westbrook Street, Stroudwater Street, a two-lane street, with over 500 more cars… This should be going off onto Rand Road.”
blocks.cite: Deborah Napier, Portland resident on Congress St. (public comment)

blocks.x: “This is the wrong development on the wrong piece of land… If the developer's design triggers localized flooding or alters the natural drainage onto adjoining agricultural fields, it creates immediate civil liability.”
blocks.cite: Beth Paulson-Omstead, reading a statement for abutting farm owner Arthur Randall (public comment)

blocks.x: Others also spoke against the Stroudwater Street access point. Woody Howard, President of the Stroudwater Neighborhood Association [1:30:37], asked whether anyone has made a direct appeal to the Maine Department of Transportation (MDOT) about reclassifying the road. Elizabeth Gateen [1:40:45] also spoke against it. Deborah Romery [1:43:43] described a line of cars already parked along Stroudwater St. from the middle school during a Sept. 22 school cross-country event. David Kent, President of the Maine Farm Bureau [1:48:42], warned the development team to proactively disclose to future tenants that they're moving next to an active farm.

“There's more to the development than just the vehicular access in and out. There is the pedestrian traffic, the bicyclists… introducing the vehicular access to the arterial is inherently introducing pedestrians and bicyclists to that as well.”

Staff explained the arterial is a "control of access" highway. The right to new access points was purchased from abutting properties when the arterial was built. So no new curb cut is legally permitted there, regardless of this project. Both MDOT and staff rule out putting pedestrians at street level with traffic on that 45-mph section, on safety grounds. Access there would require a grade-separated bridge (one that passes above or below the road), estimated at $5–10 million. Staff said its long switchbacks would discourage people from using it. Staff's position: Stroudwater Street has adequate capacity for this project's trip count. Any needed intersection improvements would come out of a separate traffic movement permit.
“I've driven down Stroudwater twice a day, every day for twenty years… you're just waiting, and that's existing traffic… that is the problem.”

Turcotte also pressed on whether the middle-school access point could truly be enforced as emergency-only. He asked for stronger buffering for neighboring homes and the Randall farm. Karen Axelson questioned why a road's access designation can't be revisited the way zoning can be. Staff clarified that the arterial is a state (not city) road. They said the access restriction was purchased as part of its original federal-aid construction. Robin Tannenbaum, seconded by Oriana Farnham, pressed the applicant team (Tuck O'Brien, JB Brown & Sons; Tyler Norad, Westbrook Development Corporation; Caleb Barassa, civil engineer) to make the affordable-housing building cluster feel less visually separated from the market-rate buildings. Chair McWilliams asked about screening and the undeveloped half of the parcel. Nancy Litrocapes asked what the open green areas would become, suggesting a bee meadow. The applicant team committed to continuing that work and to coordinating directly with the Stroudwater Neighborhood Association. It did not change the access plan on the spot.
No vote — workshop item. The project remains at the workshop stage. The next step is state permit applications, with a return to the board expected spring 2027.

This is a smaller-footprint revision of a subdivision the board approved in 2023. That subdivision had 9 lots and a private way, and its grading proved very difficult to construct. The applicant now proposes 6 duplex buildings (12 units) on ~19 wooded acres between 630 and 706

Methodist Road. Most of the parcel is left undeveloped at the rear. Board feedback focused on buffering/screening (including headlight glare toward a neighboring house) and setbacks (required distances from a property line) from Methodist Road (a 25-foot vegetative buffer plus a 30-foot structure setback). Member Kevin Price disclosed he is within the project's notification radius, though not an abutter. He offered to recuse himself, or step out of, any future vote. The board had no objection to him participating tonight.
No vote — workshop item; feedback only.

These are two ordinance amendments, part of a city-wide review of board/committee ordinances. Seven other boards were already amended by City Council on Sept. 21, 2026. The changes are to the Village Review Overlay Zone (VROZ) committee, and to Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) enforcement appeals. An overlay zone is a district with extra rules layered on top of the regular zoning. Workshop only — a public hearing and formal recommendation to City Council are planned for the November meeting.

The VROZ piece drew no opposition. Staff proposed returning VROZ architectural review authority to the Planning Board and sunsetting (ending) the VROZ committee. Longtime member Robin Tannenbaum supported this: “as a founding member… let her go. Times have changed.” The ZBA piece was different.
The proposal (Jennie Franceschi, Assistant City Administrator)

The proposal would remove a property owner's ability to appeal a Code Enforcement Officer (CEO) enforcement action to the ZBA. That path would go to Superior Court instead. Appeals of a CEO's interpretation of the ordinance, or of a permit denial/approval, would still go to the ZBA unchanged. Rationale: the City now sends separate attorneys for the CEO and the ZBA to every enforcement-action hearing. Franceschi said this has become a real cost driver.

“If you're aggrieved in any way, you have to go off to court… I think that's a bad idea… You get before the [ZBA] fast… [In court] you got 21 days to go find an attorney… I have a case now, we're seven months in.”
blocks.cite: Vice Chair John Turcotte (former ZBA member, real estate litigation attorney)

blocks.x: Turcotte argued the change would be “very selfish… on the city's behalf and to the detriment of Westbrook citizens,” since a Superior Court appeal is slower and more expensive for the resident. He also argued it would cost the City more than one night of a ZBA appeal. He said most real cases are ordinary neighbor disputes, rather than the hypothetical bad actors used to justify the policy.
“We are paying for two attorneys for every meeting now… we're getting advised from our own attorneys that this is actually in the city's best interest.”

Franceschi said the City now requires separate counsel for the CEO and the ZBA at enforcement hearings. That is not required by the current ordinance, but it is current practice. Franceschi also said the change followed specific legal advice after a run of costly cases. Kevin Price noted a “collaborative” culture could change with staff turnover even if the ordinance doesn't. That could make the restriction more consequential later. The ZBA's own chair, shown the draft in advance, asked staff to go further and remove ZBA appeals from the Shoreland Zoning section too. Staff incorporated that.
No vote — workshop/referral item. Returns to the board in November for a public hearing and formal recommendation to City Council.

Chair McWilliams noted the board's November meeting falls on Nov. 3 — Election Day — and he won't be able to attend. McWilliams is running for a State House seat. Staff (Rebecca Spitella) noted that the board had previously been directed to keep meeting on election nights. Staff said this year's date can't move because of public-noticing requirements and because the pending data-center ordinance's own timeline depends on that meeting. Staff agreed the recurring every-other-year conflict is worth revisiting for future election years.
No vote — discussion only; November 3rd meeting date stands for this year.
Revisit the Planning Board's meeting-date policy for future election years — Assignee: City Administration | Deadline: none set.
